The Board honored MPAAA award recipients, twenty retiring employees, and a Student Spotlight honoree, and adopted proclamations for National Teacher Appreciation Week and Mental Health Awareness Month. Its most consequential action was Resolution 22-047, authorizing preparation of an Application for Preliminary Qualification of Bonds to the Michigan Department of Treasury for a bond issue of not more than $555,000,000, anticipated for the November 8, 2022 ballot.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, May 17, 2022, held in the Troy School District Services Building located at 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:01 p.m.; the meeting was adjourned at 9:39 p.m. Approximately 70 members of the audience attended. Minutes signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education (GH/jh).

**Attendance**
Present: Schmidt, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Wilson. Absent: Dr. Philippart. Also present: Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Detmer, Keyser, Recker, Fulcher, Canfield, Zendler, Zawislak, and West.

**Recognitions**
- Laura Duzey, Pupil Accounting Coordinator, and Isabella Ball, Data Services Specialist, recipients of the 2022 MPAAA Outstanding Service Award, nominated by Carolyn Claerhout, Manager of Pupil Services for Oakland County.
- Troy School District retirees for the 2021-2022 school year, whose names and service start years were read by Mr. Harris; each received a gift and certificate.
- Student Spotlight: Anoush Rophael, freshman at Athens High School, recognized through the TSD Creative Guild for producing, directing, and editing a video on the annual IA-East Art Show. Thomas Butcher introduced her.

**Actions and Votes**

| No. | Item | Moved / Supported | Vote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 22-041 | National Teacher Appreciation Week resolution, May 1-7, 2022 | Hammond / Gottlieb | Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart |
| 22-042 | Mental Health Awareness Month proclamation (Oakland Community Health Network) | Wilson / Anne | Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart |
| 22-043 | Consent agenda items A through H | Hauff / Anne | Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart |
| 22-044 | Two-year administrative contract without tenure to Mrs. Amy Wallace, Principal, Wattles Elementary, beginning 2022-23 | Gottlieb / Hammond | Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart |
| 22-045 | Replacement computers for secondary labs, $476,985.00 from the 2019 Capital Projects Fund | Hammond / Gottlieb | Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart |
| 22-046 | Stadium lighting contract to Airport Lighting Employee-Owned LLC, $652,278.00 from the 2019 Capital Projects Funds | Anne / Hauff | Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart |
| 22-047 | Resolution relating to preliminary qualification of the proposed bond issue, not more than $555,000,000 | Hauff / Anne | Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart |
| 22-048 | 2022 Oakland Schools Board election resolution under Public Act 419 of 2004 | Schmidt / Anne | Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart |

**Consent Agenda (22-043)**
Minutes of the April 5, 2022 Board Workshop; minutes of the April 19, 2022 Board Meeting; Treasurer's Report for March 2022; approval of the Oakland Intermediate School District budget; resolution to hold a public hearing on the proposed 2022/2023 school year budget; food service contract renewal; and IA Okma Campus budget approval for the 2022/2023 school year.

**Bond and Facilities Report**
Facilities Review Committee members updated the Board on the upcoming bond proposal. Matt Sackrison described the methodology of the community survey gauging willingness to vote for a bond proposal and potential millage increases; Scott Courtney and Alison Hendry reported FRC feedback and top priorities for additional spending, including which buildings most need improvements. Discussion covered state qualified bonds, effects on taxpayers, and interest rates. Resolution 22-047 authorized administration to work with the District's architect, construction manager, bond counsel, and financial advisor on an Application for Preliminary Qualification under the School Bond Qualification and Loan Program, with the proposal anticipated for the Regular School Election of November 8, 2022.

**Public Communication and Reports**
Speakers included Tracy Owens, Ashleigh Jennings, Ollie Apahidean, Sarah Krieger, Jeff Schaeper, Kelly Jones, and Sarah Primeau. Student representatives reporting were Alyssa McLarty (Troy College and Career High School), Yara Mashal (International Academy-East), Hannah DiGiovanni (Athens High School, in for Sasha Palmkoeck), and Sarayu Bethamcherla (Troy High School).
2022_254_m051722bdmtg.verbose:
Official minutes of the regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education held Tuesday, May 17, 2022, in the Troy School District Services Building located at 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:01 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, and Wilson were present; Dr. Philippart was absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Detmer, Keyser, Recker, Fulcher, Canfield, Zendler, Zawislak, and West. There were approximately 70 members of the audience. The meeting was adjourned at 9:39 p.m., and the minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typist notation GH/jh.

RECOGNITIONS. The TSD Mission Moment honored Laura Duzey, Pupil Accounting Coordinator, and Isabella Ball, Data Services Specialist, recipients of the 2022 MPAAA Outstanding Service Award. They were nominated by Carolyn Claerhout, Manager of Pupil Services for Oakland County. The citation credited their leadership through the pupil accounting process, their integrity and commitment to the rules, and their internal and external relationship-building, which aided in maximizing student counts and obtaining clean pupil accounting audits.

The Board next recognized Troy School District employees who retired or announced their intention to retire at the end of the 2021-2022 school year. Mr. Harris read each name and length of service: Joyce Brasington (Principal, Wattles Elementary, since 2013); Cheryl Buxton (Teacher, Hamilton Elementary, since 2012); John Fedyk (Workforce Staff, Troy Career Center, since 1998); Tatiana Godlewski (Teacher, Athens, since 2000); Dawn Hayes (Teacher, Athens, since 1995); Kathy Hoppe (Secretary, Troy Learning Center, since 2016); Lois Hurdle (Secretary, Services Building, since 2000); Lynda Keough (Workforce Staff, Troy Career Center, since 2002); Jackie Kochanski (Para-Professional, TSD Preschool, since 2008); Laura Laga (Secretary, Services, since 2014); Jeff McCoy (Teacher, Martell/Morse, since 2000); Jane McKenney (Teacher, Baker Middle School, since 1981); John Morrison (Teacher, Troy High, since 1998); Brad Morton (Teacher, Athens, since 1990); Jane Moss (Teacher, Athens, since 1993); Tammy Polena (Teacher, Schroeder, since 1987); Rick Rinnan (Counselor, Athens, since 2000); Cheryl Schubeck (Workforce Staff, Troy Career Center, since 2007); Rosanne Thomas (Teacher, Barnard/Wattles, since 2004); and Rita Ward (Teacher, Morse, since 1989). Each retiree received congratulations from the Board along with a gift and certificate.

The monthly Student Spotlight recognized Anoush Rophael, a freshman at Athens High School, for work produced through the TSD Creative Guild. She produced, directed, and edited a video focused on the annual IA-East Art Show and the work of seniors over their four years in the art program. Thomas Butcher was invited to speak about Anoush and to share her video; she received praise from the Board and a certificate.

RESOLUTION 22-041, NATIONAL TEACHER APPRECIATION WEEK. Moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mr. Gottlieb, reciting that teachers inspire and nurture children, promote democratic equality, develop leaders, encourage critical thinking, and set the bar for excellence, and resolving that the Troy School District supports National Teacher Appreciation Week, May 1-7, 2022, and encourages schools and community to recognize the role of teachers. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

RESOLUTION 22-042, 2022 MENTAL HEALTH AWARENESS MONTH. Introduced in connection with Oakland Community Health Network (OCHN), which with its service provider network hosts initiatives promoting community awareness of mental illness and asked Oakland County school boards to approve a May proclamation. Moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Anne. Recitals noted the COVID-19 pandemic's reminder about integrating mental health into preparedness and public health response plans; disproportionately worse mental health outcomes, increased substance use, and elevated suicidal ideation among younger adults, racial/ethnic minorities, essential workers, and adult caregivers; the World Health Organization statistic that as many as one in six U.S. children ages 6-17 has a treatable mental health disorder such as depression, anxiety problems, or ADHD; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data that between 2016-2019 approximately 5.8 million children ages 3-17 years were diagnosed with anxiety and 2.7 million were diagnosed with depression; the designation of May 5, 2022 as National Children's Mental Health Awareness Day and May 1 through May 7, 2022 as Children's Mental Health Awareness Week; and OCHN's commitment to being a Zero Suicide organization. The resolution recognized May 2022 as Mental Health Awareness Month. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS: none. PUBLIC COMMUNICATION on agenda items: none.

CONSENT AGENDA, 22-043. Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Anne, approving items A through H: minutes of the April 5, 2022 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the April 19, 2022 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report for March 2022; approval of the Oakland Intermediate School District Budget; a resolution to hold a public hearing on the proposed 2022/2023 school year budget; food service contract renewal; and IA Okma Campus budget approval for the 2022/2023 school year. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

PERSONNEL, 22-044. Moved by Mr. Gottlieb and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the Board issue a two-year administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Mrs. Amy Wallace, who will begin duties as Principal, Wattles Elementary, commencing with the 2022-23 school year. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. CURRICULUM: none.

BUSINESS, 22-045, SECONDARY COMPUTER LABS. Moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mr. Gottlieb that replacement computers for the secondary labs be awarded as attached in the amount of $476,985.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

BUSINESS, 22-046, STADIUM LIGHTING. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Hauff that the contract for new stadium lighting be awarded to Airport Lighting Employee-Owned LLC in the amount of $652,278.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Funds. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

REPORT, FACILITIES REVIEW COMMITTEE BOND UPDATE. Members of the Facilities Review Committee updated the Board on the upcoming bond proposal. Matt Sackrison shared the methodology of the community survey conducted to gauge interest and willingness to vote for a bond proposal and potential millage increases. Scott Courtney and Alison Hendry provided FRC feedback and shared top priorities for additional spending, discussing which buildings were most in need of improvements. Board members asked questions about the FRC surveys, findings, and recommendations, and discussed the upcoming bond proposal, state qualified bonds, the effect on taxpayers, and interest rates.

RESOLUTION 22-047, PRELIMINARY QUALIFICATION OF THE PROPOSED BOND ISSUE. Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Anne. Recitals stated the School District had considered capital improvement projects described in Exhibit A (the Proposed Projects), considered requesting voter approval for capital improvement bonds, and intended to request preliminary qualification from the Michigan Department of Treasury in order to qualify the bonds under the School Bond Qualification and Loan Program, noting that the Department requires the scope, dollar amount, and number of bond proposals to be determined before reviewing a draft application. The Board authorized administration to work with the District's architect, construction manager, bond counsel, financial advisor, and other professionals in preparing an Application for Preliminary Qualification of Bonds for submission to the Department, and to meet with Department representatives before final Board approval at a future meeting. The total amount of bonds to finance the Proposed Projects shall be not more than five hundred fifty-five million dollars ($555,000,000). The Board anticipated the bonds may be issued in one or more series and expected to submit the proposal to the electors at the Regular School Election to be held November 8, 2022. Conflicting resolutions were rescinded. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart; the resolution was declared adopted. A certification by the Secretary attests the resolution was adopted at a regular meeting held May 17, 2022 in compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION. Mrs. Tracy Owens, Troy resident and parent, addressed ESSER funds, spring tutoring, and the curriculum used to teach reading. Ms. Ashleigh Jennings spoke in support of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion and a safe, inclusive environment. Mr. Ollie Apahidean raised parental rights, concerns about indoctrination, and books available in District media centers. Mrs. Sarah Krieger raised concerns about the content of books in District libraries and read an excerpt. Mr. Jeff Schaeper described a recent meeting with administration. Mrs. Kelly Jones thanked the Board, teachers, staff, and student representatives. Ms. Sarah Primeau, parent of a junior, addressed Mental Health Awareness Month and was informed the resolution had already passed.

STUDENT REPRESENTATIVE REPORTS. Alyssa McLarty (Troy College and Career High School), Yara Mashal (International Academy-East), Hannah DiGiovanni (Athens High School, filling in for Sasha Palmkoeck), and Sarayu Bethamcherla (Troy High School).

OTHER, 22-048, 2022 OAKLAND SCHOOLS BOARD ELECTION. Moved by Mr. Schmidt and supported by Mrs. Anne, reciting Public Act 419 of 2004, which amended election procedures for Intermediate School Districts electing board members at a meeting of constituent district representatives and requires a constituent board to designate its representative and identify the candidate it supports by resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days prior to the election, considered at not less than one public meeting. The Board designated Gary Hauff as its representative and Vital Anne as alternate on the 2022 electoral body for the Oakland Schools Intermediate School District Board of Education; supported candidate Steve Gottlieb for the two positions, each for a term of six years ending June 30, 2028; and directed Gary Hauff to vote for Steve Gottlieb for both candidate positions at least on the first ballot at the June 6, 2022 election. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. The attached certification text references a regular meeting held on May 19, 2020.

BOARD COMMENTS. Mrs. Hammond expressed appreciation for teachers. Mr. Gottlieb thanked the student representatives and colleagues for support in the upcoming OISD election ballot. Mrs. Anne thanked teachers and described a professional development session showing job-embedded learning by third grade teachers. Mr. Hauff announced a Preschool Summer Camp at the Troy Learning Center from June 20 through August 12. Dr. Wilson thanked Troy teachers and endorsed the District's professional development. Dr. Machesky thanked the Facilities Review Committee, announced the TFEE Golf Outing on Friday, June 17 at Sanctuary Lake Golf Course with proceeds going back into classrooms, stated the District is not abandoning AP coursework and no changes will be made for the 2022-23 school year, and explained that course reviews broaden opportunities for students. Mr. Schmidt reported participating in APT to Succeed at Larson, discussed improvements in Reading Recovery efforts and improved reading proficiency scores for disadvantaged and special education students, and announced the next Board Workshop for June 14 at 6:00 p.m. in the Administration Building and the regular Board Meeting for June 21 at 7:00 p.m. at the Services Building.

Resolution Approving Bond Proposition to Be Voted On at the General School Election, prepared for the Board of Education of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, Michigan, at a regular meeting held in the School District on the 26th day of July, 2022, at 9:00 a.m. local time. RECITALS. The School District is contemplating undertaking various capital improvements to facilities within the School District, which include remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields, playgrounds and other facilities; erecting and completing, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom room additions and other additions to existing school buildings and other facilities; acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment in school buildings and other facilities; and acquiring sites, preparing, developing and improving sites at school buildings and other facilities and the purchase of school buses, collectively defined as the Projects. The School District is of the opinion that in order to finance the Projects, a bonding proposition should be submitted to the electors at the General School Election to be held November 8, 2022. The School District is a Michigan general powers school district operating under the Revised School Code, as amended, and as such its elections are governed by the Michigan Election Law, Act 116, Public Acts of Michigan, 1954, as amended. The election will be conducted by the School District's Election Coordinator, the Clerk of the County of Oakland. Michigan Election Law requires the School District to certify ballot language for any proposals submitted for voter approval at an allowable election date to the Election Coordinator not later than 4:00 p.m. on the twelfth Tuesday before the election date. The School District desires to approve the bonding proposition and to authorize the Superintendent or his designee to certify it to the Election Coordinator.

RESOLVED CLAUSES. (1) The School Improvement Bond Proposal attached as Exhibit A is approved and shall be submitted to the electors at the General School Election to be held on November 8, 2022. (2) The Superintendent or his designee are authorized to certify the Proposal to the School District's Election Coordinator, the Clerk of the County of Oakland, on or before 4:00 p.m. on August 16, 2022, which is not later than the twelfth Tuesday before the General School Election to be held on November 8, 2022. (3) The Superintendent or his designee are further authorized to take any and all action required under Michigan Election Law with regard to the General School Election to be held on November 8, 2022. (4) All resolutions and parts of resolutions insofar as they conflict with the provisions of this Resolution are rescinded. The form then states RESOLUTION DECLARED ADOPTED.

CERTIFICATION. The undersigned duly qualified and acting Secretary of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, Michigan, Gary Hauff, certifies that the foregoing is a true and complete copy of a Resolution adopted by the Board of Education at a regular meeting held on July 26, 2022, the original of which is part of the Board's minutes, and further certifies that notice of the meeting was given to the public under the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, as amended.

OFFICIAL BALLOT, TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT, COUNTY OF OAKLAND, STATE OF MICHIGAN, SCHOOL IMPROVEMENT BOND PROPOSITION. The ballot asks: Shall the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, borrow the sum of not to exceed Five Hundred Fifty-Five Million Dollars ($555,000,000) and issue its general obligation unlimited tax bonds, in one or more series, for the purpose of paying for the cost of the following projects: remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing, re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields, playgrounds and other facilities to create a modern learning environment for students and for health, safety, security and other purposes; erecting, completing, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom additions and other additions to existing school buildings and other facilities; acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment in school buildings and other facilities; and acquiring sites, preparing, developing and improving sites at school buildings and other facilities and the purchase of school buses. The ballot provides YES and NO choices.

BALLOT DISCLOSURES. The annual debt millage required to retire all bonds of the School District currently outstanding and proposed pursuant to the ballot is expected to be at or below 6.10 mills, which is a 2 mill increase from the 4.10 mills of annual debt millage levied in 2022. The maximum number of years any series of bonds may be outstanding, exclusive of refunding, is not more than thirty (30) years. The estimated millage that will be levied to pay the proposed bonds in the first year is 3.35 mills, which is equal to $3.35 per $1,000 of taxable value. The estimated simple average annual millage that will be required to retire each series of bonds is 3.94 mills annually, or $3.94 per $1,000 of taxable value.

STATE GUARANTEE. If approved by the voters, the bonds will be guaranteed by the State under the School Bond Qualification and Loan Program. The School District currently has $104,165,000 of qualified bonds outstanding and $0 of qualified loans outstanding under the Program. The School District does not expect to borrow from the Program to pay debt service on these bonds. The estimated computed millage rate required to be levied to pay the proposed bonds may change in the future based on changes in certain circumstances. A parenthetical closing note states that pursuant to State law, expenditure of bond proceeds must be audited, and the proceeds cannot be used for teacher, administrator or employee salaries, repair or maintenance costs or other operating expenses.

2022_257_8a_fs_lunch_prices_1.paragraph: Federal Food and Nutrition Service guidance, dated February 2022 and included in the July 26, 2022 Troy Board of Education packet, explaining the Paid Lunch Equity calculations School Food Authorities must perform for School Year 2022-23 in the contiguous States. School Food Authorities whose weighted average paid lunch price in SY 2021-22 fell below the target weighted average price of $3.31 must either raise their weighted average lunch price or add non-Federal funds to the non-profit school food service account. The guidance also describes the non-Federal source contribution calculation, credit and shortfall carryover, and the data inputs required by the accompanying SY 2022-23 PLE Tool.
2022_257_8a_fs_lunch_prices_1.page:
**Purpose**
Guidance on the calculations School Food Authorities (SFAs) can use to ensure compliance with Paid Lunch Equity (PLE) requirements for School Year (SY) 2022-23. The tool described is for the contiguous States. Dated February 2022.

**SY 2022-23 Paid Lunch Equity Calculation**
For SY 2022-23, SFAs which, on a weighted average, charged less than the target weighted average price for paid lunches in SY 2021-22 must adjust their weighted average lunch price or add non-Federal funds to the non-profit school food service account.

| Target weighted average paid lunch price | Area |
|---|---|
| $3.31 | contiguous States |
| $3.87 | Hawaii, Guam, The U.S. Virgin Islands, and Puerto Rico |
| $5.37 | Alaska |

SFAs must use their unrounded adjusted average paid lunch price requirement from SY 2021-22 when calculating the weighted average lunch price increase for SY 2022-23. The guidance gives an example in which the unrounded SY 2021-22 requirement was $2.98 but the SFA opted to round down to $2.95. If an SFA raised its weighted average paid lunch price above the required amount in SY 2021-22, that excess may be subtracted from the total SY 2022-23 requirement; a shortfall carries the other direction. SFAs must keep sufficient records to document and carry forward the weighted average price calculations.

**Use of Non-Federal Sources**
SFAs that contribute non-Federal sources to the nonprofit school food service account in lieu of raising paid lunch prices determine the total number of paid reimbursable lunches claimed for the previous school year and multiply that by the difference between the SY 2021-22 weighted average paid lunch price requirement and the SY 2021-22 weighted average paid lunch price. Beginning in SY 2013-14, FNS expanded the definition of a non-Federal source. For SY 2022-23, SFAs may continue to count as a non-Federal source: (1) per-meal non-Federal reimbursement for any paid meal, including breakfast and lunch; (2) any funds provided by organizations for any paid meal; and (3) any proportion attributable to paid meals from direct payments made from school district funds to support lunch service.

**Credit for Excess Non-Federal Funds**
If an SFA's SY 2021-22 estimate of the required contribution exceeded the actual level, the excess may be subtracted from the SY 2022-23 requirement; if the estimate was less than required, additional non-Federal funds must be added. The non-Federal Calculator tab applies the same crediting rationale used for paid lunch prices.

**SY 2022-23 PLE Tool**
The first tab contains detailed instructions, which users are advised to print and read first. The Tool calculates the weighted average paid lunch price for SY 2021-22, the required average weighted paid lunch price increase for SY 2022-23, and the required non-Federal source contribution for SY 2022-23, accounting for credits or shortfalls accrued. A split feature allows SFAs to meet the requirement by both raising prices and contributing non-Federal funds.

**Data Needed**
All SFAs: the SY 2021-22 unrounded price requirement, or the SY 2010-11 weighted average price, or the most recent unrounded figure; all paid lunch prices for October 2021; and the number of paid lunches served associated with each paid lunch price in October 2021. SFAs contributing non-Federal sources also need the total number of paid lunches served in SY 2021-2022 and the total dollar amount of non-Federal contributions for SY 2011-12, SY 2012-13, SY 2013-14, SY 2014-15, SY 2015-16, SY 2016-17, SY 2017-18, SY 2018-19, SY 2019-2020, SY 2020-2021, and SY 2021-2022. The Tool includes a report SFAs can print and retain for their SY 2023-24 calculations.
2022_257_8a_fs_lunch_prices_1.verbose:
Federal guidance document included as item 8A in the July 26, 2022 Troy Board of Education packet, titled in the packet as FS Lunch Prices_1 and dated February 2022. It provides guidance on the calculations School Food Authorities (SFAs) can use in order to ensure they are in compliance with the Paid Lunch Equity requirements for School Year (SY) 2022-23, and states that the tool described is for the contiguous States.

SY 2022-23 PAID LUNCH EQUITY CALCULATIONS. For SY 2022-23, SFAs which, on a weighted average, charged less than the target weighted average price of $3.31 for paid lunches in SY 2021-22 are required to adjust their weighted average lunch price or add non-Federal funds to the non-profit school food service account. The corresponding target weighted average prices for other areas are $3.87 in Hawaii, Guam, The U.S. Virgin Islands, and Puerto Rico, and $5.37 in Alaska. SFAs are reminded that they must use their unrounded adjusted average paid lunch price requirement from SY 2021-22 when calculating the weighted average lunch price increase for SY 2022-23. The guidance offers the example that if the unrounded SY 2021-22 requirement was $2.98 but the SFA opted to round down to $2.95, the calculation of the SY 2022-23 requirement is based on the unrounded figure. If an SFA raised its weighted average paid lunch price above the required amount in SY 2021-22, that excess paid lunch price increase may be subtracted from the total SY 2022-23 paid lunch price increase requirement. SFAs must keep sufficient records to document and carry forward the weighted average price calculations. If an SFA did not raise its weighted average adjusted paid lunch price sufficiently to meet the required amount in SY 2021-22, the shortfall carries forward.

USE OF NON-FEDERAL SOURCES CALCULATION. SFAs that choose to contribute non-Federal sources to the nonprofit school food service account in lieu of raising paid lunch prices must calculate the appropriate amount to contribute. To determine the amount of required revenue in lieu of a paid lunch price increase, the SFA determines the total number of paid reimbursable lunches claimed for the previous school year and multiplies that by the difference between the SY 2021-22 weighted average paid lunch price requirement and the SY 2021-22 weighted average paid lunch price.

SOURCES OF NON-FEDERAL FUNDS. Beginning in SY 2013-14, FNS expanded the definition of a non-Federal source to include all paid meals, in order to help SFAs meet the PLE requirement and to acknowledge continuing support by States and localities to improve access to and participation in the breakfast program; FNS reports having received positive response to this flexibility. Therefore, for SY 2022-23, SFAs may continue to count as a non-Federal source: (1) per-meal non-Federal reimbursement for any paid meal, such as breakfast or lunch; (2) any funds provided by organizations for any paid meal; and (3) any proportion attributable to paid meals from direct payments made from school district funds to support lunch service.

CREDIT FOR EXCESS NON-FEDERAL FUNDS. If an SFA's SY 2021-22 estimate of the required contribution exceeded the actual level, that excess contribution may be subtracted from the total SY 2022-23 contribution requirement. If the SY 2021-22 estimate was less than required, additional funds from non-Federal sources must be added. The non-Federal Calculator tab in the PLE Tool, used to determine the estimated amount of non-Federal source contributions, allows these calculations using the same rationale applied to paid lunch prices, crediting extra funds contributed and accounting for shortfalls when determining the non-Federal funds requirement for the next school year.

SY 2022-23 PLE TOOL. The first tab of the SY 2022-23 PLE Tool includes detailed instructions on how to use the tool and what information is needed to complete the appropriate calculations; each user is recommended to print and read the instructions before attempting the calculations. The attached SY 2022-23 PLE Tool makes the following calculations: the weighted average paid lunch price for SY 2021-22; the required average weighted paid lunch price increase for SY 2022-23; and the required non-Federal source contribution for SY 2022-23. The Tool takes into account adjustments to paid lunch prices made by the SFA in SY 2021-22 to calculate any credit or shortfall accrued for SY 2022-23, and for SFAs that opted to contribute non-Federal funds it also calculates credits and shortfalls for the SY 2022-23 required non-Federal contribution. The Tool additionally includes a feature that makes calculations for SFAs wishing to split the SY 2022-23 requirement by both raising prices and contributing non-Federal funds, an option described as potentially attractive to SFAs that do not want to raise the weighted average paid lunch price by the entire required amount.

REQUIRED DATA INPUTS. All SFAs need the following data to calculate the Weighted Average Price for SY 2022-23: the SY 2021-22 unrounded price requirement, or the SY 2010-11 weighted average price, or the most recent unrounded figure; all paid lunch prices for October 2021; and the number of paid lunches served associated with each paid lunch price in October 2021. SFAs that have opted to contribute non-Federal sources also need the total number of paid lunches served in SY 2021-2022 and the total dollar amount of non-Federal contributions for SY 2011-12, SY 2012-13, SY 2013-14, SY 2014-15, SY 2015-16, SY 2016-17, SY 2017-18, SY 2018-19, SY 2019-2020, SY 2020-2021, and SY 2021-2022. SFAs wishing to split the SY 2022-23 requirement by both raising paid lunch prices and contributing non-Federal sources need all of the above information. The PLE Tool also includes a report SFAs can use to track the information needed for their SY 2023-24 calculations, which they can print and keep in their records.

2022_258_8a_fs_lunch_prices_2.paragraph: Instruction sheet for the School Year 2022-23 Paid Lunch Equity (PLE) Tool, dated February 2022 and attached as item 8A of the July 26, 2022 Troy Board of Education packet, with a blank SFA NAME field at the top. The Tool helps School Food Authorities calculate their paid lunch price increase requirement and/or non-Federal source contributions to meet the requirements specified in 7 CFR 210.14(e), and computes credits or deficits carried into the following year. It walks users through three alternative methods, raising prices, contributing non-Federal sources, or a split of both, and notes that the $0.10 cap does not mean every SFA will raise prices or contribute that amount.
2022_258_8a_fs_lunch_prices_2.page:
**Document**
School Year (SY) 2022-23 Paid Lunch Equity (PLE) Tool Instructions, dated February 2022, with a blank SFA NAME field. Users are advised they may want to print the instructions and use them while working through the Tool. This version of the PLE Tool applies only to SY 2022-23; a new version will be issued for SY 2023-24.

**Purpose and Authority**
The PLE Tool was created to help School Food Authorities (SFAs) calculate their paid lunch price increase requirement and/or non-Federal source contributions to meet the requirements specified in 7 CFR 210.14(e). If the pricing requirements calculated by the Tool are not met or are exceeded, the Tool also calculates any amounts, including credits or deficits, carried over into the next year. The weighted average prices calculated are the weighted average of all student paid lunch prices charged in the SFA. For more information on amounts carried over, the instructions refer to FNS Policy Memo SP 39-2011 (revised).

**Tips Listed**
1) Have the most recent year PLE tool completed available for reference. 2) Did the SFA have credits carried over from prior years? 3) Is the most recent weighted average paid lunch price above the requirement? 4) Only the tab(s) relevant to the SFA's selected method need to be completed. 5) The $0.10 cap does not mean that every SFA will raise the weighted average paid lunch price or contribute the equivalent in non-Federal funds; depending on where the SFA stands, less than $0.10 may be required or the SFA may choose to contribute more.

**Tab Structure**
The instructions state the SY 2022-23 PLE Tool consists of 8 tabs, with hyperlinks placed throughout for navigation.

| Tab | Content |
|---|---|
| Tab 1 | Instructions |
| Tab 2 | Annual Unrounded Requirement Finder |
| Tab 3 | SY 2022-23 Price Calculator / Price Adjustment Calculator |
| Tab 4 | SY 2022-23 Non-Federal Calculator |
| Tab 5 | SY 2022-23 Split Calculator |
| Tab 6 | SY 2022-23 REPORT |
| Tab 7 | SY 21-22 Price Calculator (optional, as needed) |
| Tab 8 | SY 10-11 Price Calculator (optional, as needed) |
| Tab 9 | PLE Guidance |

Shaded cells designate data entry cells that the SFA must complete for the tool to calculate requirements.

**Data Required**
To calculate the Weighted Average Price for SY 2022-23: the SY 2021-22 Weighted Average Price; the SY 2010-11 Weighted Average Price if the SY 2021-22 figure is unknown; all student paid lunch prices for October 2021; and the number of paid lunches served associated with each student paid lunch price in October 2021. SFAs that opted to contribute non-Federal sources also need the SY 2010-11 Weighted Average Price as needed, the SY 2021-22 Weighted Average Price if different, the total number of student paid lunches served in SY 2020-21, and the total dollar amount of non-Federal contributions through SY 2021-22.

**Method Walkthroughs**
Weighted average price method: enter the SY 2021-22 unrounded price requirement in the orange box (using the annual unrounded requirement finder if unknown), then enter October 2021 student paid lunch counts and prices in the Price Calculator; the tool computes amounts needed to meet SY 2022-23 requirements and amounts carried forward to SY 2023-24. An optional Pricing Estimation Calculator lets the SFA vary individual prices until the weighted average reaches the new requirement. Non-Federal source method: enter the unrounded requirement, the current weighted average student paid lunch price, the student paid lunch count for the entire 2020-21 school year, and the amount of non-Federal source funds contributed from SY 2011-12 through SY 2021-22; the tool applies the $0.10 cap if applicable and computes the remaining annual contribution for SY 2022-23, the remaining contribution carried forward to SY 2023-24, and remaining credit carried forward. Split method: combines both, with a New Price Increase entry for the weighted average price the SFA plans to charge in SY 2022-23. Optional tabs 7 and 8 support calculations from previous years.
2022_258_8a_fs_lunch_prices_2.verbose:
School Year (SY) 2022-23 Paid Lunch Equity (PLE) Tool Instructions, dated February 2022, attached as item 8A to the July 26, 2022 Troy Board of Education agenda. The sheet opens with a blank SFA NAME field and a note that users may want to print the instructions and use them as they work their way through the PLE Tool.

PURPOSE. The PLE Tool was created to help School Food Authorities (SFAs) calculate their paid lunch price increase requirement and/or non-Federal source contributions to meet the requirements specified in 7 CFR 210.14(e). If the pricing requirements calculated by the PLE Tool are not met or are exceeded, the PLE Tool will also calculate any amounts, including credits or deficits, carried over into the next year. The weighted average prices calculated in the PLE Tool are the weighted average of all student paid lunch prices charged in the SFA.

TIPS. The instructions list five tips: (1) have the most recent year PLE tool you completed available for reference; (2) did the SFA have credits carried over from prior years; (3) is the most recent weighted average paid lunch price above the requirement; (4) only the tab or tabs relevant to the SFA's selection of method to meet PLE requirements need to be completed; and (5) the $0.10 cap does not mean that every SFA will raise the weighted average paid lunch price or contribute the equivalent in non-Federal funds, since depending on where the SFA is relative to meeting the PLE requirement, a contribution of less than $0.10 may be required or the SFA may choose to contribute more than $0.10. For more information on amounts carried over, the document refers to FNS Policy Memo SP 39-2011 (revised). This version of the PLE Tool applies only to SY 2022-23; a new version of the PLE Tool will be issued for SY 2023-24.

TAB STRUCTURE. The instructions state that the SY 2022-23 PLE Tool consists of 8 tabs, with hyperlinks placed throughout the tool to navigate between them, and that only the tabs for the selected method have to be completed. The tabs identified are Tab 1: Instructions; Tab 2: Annual Unrounded Requirement Finder; Tab 3: SY 2022-23 Price Calculator, also referenced as the SY 2022-23 Price Adjustment Calculator; Tab 4: SY 2022-23 Non-Federal Calculator; Tab 5: SY 2022-23 Split Calculator; Tab 6: SY 2022-23 REPORT; Tab 7: SY 21-22 Price Calculator; Tab 8: SY 10-11 Price Calculator; and Tab 9: PLE Guidance. The SY 21-22 and SY 10-11 Price Calculator tabs are for use as needed. Shaded cells designate data entry cells, and the SFA must enter the applicable data in those cells for the tool to calculate requirements. Only the tabs for the method used to meet the requirement, raising prices, contributing non-Federal sources, or the split calculator, should be completed.

DATA NEEDED. SFAs need the following data to calculate the Weighted Average Price for SY 2022-23: (1) the SY 2021-22 Weighted Average Price; (2) the SY 2010-11 Weighted Average Price, if the SY 2021-22 Weighted Average Price is unknown; (3) all student paid lunch prices for October 2021; and (4) the number of paid lunches served associated with each student paid lunch price in October 2021. SFAs that opted to contribute non-Federal sources for SY 2022-23 need: (1) the SY 2010-11 Weighted Average Price, as needed; (2) the SY 2021-22 Weighted Average Price, if different from the SY 2010-11 Weighted Average Price; (3) the total number of student paid lunches served in SY 2020-21; and (4) the total dollar amount of non-Federal contributions through SY 2021-22.

WEIGHTED AVERAGE PAID LUNCH PRICE CALCULATION. Step 1 directs the user to enter the SY 2021-22 unrounded price requirement in the orange box, using the annual unrounded requirement finder if that requirement is not known; this figure sets the pricing requirements throughout the Tool and helps determine amounts carried forward, and was calculated through the SY 2021-22 PLE Tool. After calculating the SY 2022-23 weighted average price requirement for student paid lunches, the user clicks the link to the SY 2022-23 Price Calculator. In Step 2, the box at the top of the tab displays the SY 2022-23 Weighted Average Price Requirement; to calculate the SY 2021-22 Weighted Average Price, the SFA enters the student paid lunch count for October 2021 associated with each paid meal price in the Monthly # of Paid Lunches column, and enters each student paid lunch price in the SFA, including all schools such as elementary, middle, and high, for October 2021 in the Paid Lunch Price column. Using the SY 2021-22 weighted average price, the tool calculates amounts necessary to meet the SY 2022-23 weighted average price requirements and any amounts carried forward to SY 2023-24. A report is generated for use in the SY 2022-23 PLE tool displaying the SY 2022-23 requirements and any amount carried forward as determined on the SY 2022-23 Price Calculator, and the user selects the SY 2022-23 method used to ensure sufficient funds are provided for paid lunches.

OPTIONAL STEP 3, PRICING ESTIMATION CALCULATOR. After calculating the SY 2022-23 average student paid lunch price requirement, the PLE tool can be used to determine how the SFA wants to distribute the price increase within the SFA to reach the new average paid lunch price. The SFA enters the student paid lunch count for October 2021 associated with each student paid meal price in the Monthly # of Paid Lunches column, then changes individual student paid lunch prices until the average student paid lunch price reaches the new average requirement, which appears in the Weighted Average Price box. SFAs have flexibility to raise individual student prices using many different price combinations so that the weighted average student price equals the new SY 2022-23 required level.

NON-FEDERAL SOURCE CONTRIBUTION CALCULATION. Step 1 again requires entry of the SY 2021-22 unrounded price requirement in the orange box, with the annual unrounded requirement finder available if unknown; this figure was calculated through the SY 2021-22 PLE Tool. After calculating the SY 2022-23 weighted average price requirement for paid lunches, the user goes to the SY 2022-23 Non-Federal Source Calculator tab. In Step 2, the box at the top of the tab displays the SY 2021-22 Weighted Average Price Requirement. The user enters the current weighted average student paid lunch price, which may be the same as the SY 2021-22 weighted average price determined on the Unrounded Requirement Finder tab if the SFA did not raise the weighted average price in SY 2021-2022; the most current average weighted price can be determined on the SY 2021-2022 Price Calculator tab. The user then enters the student paid lunch count for the entire 2020-21 School Year in the orange Annual # of Paid Lunches box in the Non-Federal Source Contribution Calculator for SY 2022-23, and enters the amount of non-Federal source funds contributed for SY 2011-12 through SY 2021-22 in the orange box labeled as such. The Tool calculates the annual non-Federal source contribution for SY 2022-23 and applies the $0.10 cent cap if applicable. Based on the actual amount contributed for SY 2021-22, the tool calculates the remaining annual non-Federal source contribution for SY 2022-23, the remaining annual non-Federal source contribution carried forward to SY 2023-24, and the remaining credit carried forward to SY 2023-24.

SPLIT CALCULATOR. This tab is for SFAs wishing to split their requirement by both raising prices and contributing non-Federal sources. Step 1 enters the SY 2021-22 unrounded price requirement; Step 2 displays the SY 2022-23 Weighted Average Price Requirement and requires entry of October 2021 student paid lunch counts and each student paid lunch price across all schools; Step 3 requires entry of the weighted average price the SFA plans to charge for student paid lunches in SY 2022-23 in the New Price Increase field; and Step 4 requires entry of the student paid lunch count for the entire 2020-2021 School Year in the orange Annual # of Paid Lunches box and the actual amount of the non-Federal source contribution in the orange box labeled Amount of Non-Federal Source Funds Contributed from SY 2011-12 through SY 2021-22. The tool then calculates the remaining annual non-Federal source contribution for SY 2022-23, the remaining annual contribution carried forward to SY 2023-24, and the remaining credit carried forward to SY 2023-24. SFAs may use optional tabs 7 and 8 to make calculations from previous years.
